column1: # topic: Chapter 5: The Mosaic of Eighteenth-Century America

column2: Jean L'Archevêque was a tattooed Frenchman who helped kill La Salle in Texas, became a trusted settler of Spanish New Mexico, and died fighting Pawnees for Spain.
Don Pedro de Villasur was New Mexico's lieutenant governor who led Spanish soldiers and Pueblo Indians onto the Plains to confront the French and was killed by Pawnees.
The Pawnees were Plains Indians armed with French guns who raided the Apaches and destroyed Villasur's Spanish expedition on the Platte River.
The Caddos were sedentary farmers of east Texas who tattooed L'Archevêque, barely tolerated Spanish missions, and preferred trading with the French of Louisiana.
La Salle was the French explorer who tried to plant a colony near the Mississippi's mouth, landed in Texas instead, and was killed by his own colonists, alarming Spain.
The Apaches were the first great Indian threat to Spanish Texas and New Mexico, raiding herds and settlements until the Comanches drove most of them off the Plains.
The Comanches, who called themselves Numunuu ("the People"), became mounted warriors with European horses and French guns and dominated the southern Plains.
Ecueracapa was the Comanche leader who helped broker peace with Spain, after which the allies pressed other Indians into peace and New Mexico prospered.
Gaspar de Portolá was the pragmatic military commander who, with Junípero Serra, led the expedition that founded Spanish California's first presidios and missions.
Fray Junípero Serra was the iron-willed Franciscan who led the missionary side of the expedition that founded San Diego and Monterey in California.
Le Pesant was an Ottawa leader whose followers killed a priest and a French soldier near Fort Detroit, settled by a staged trial and escape that became a model compromise.
The Ottawas were Algonquian-speaking allies of New France who offered Indian slaves to "raise" the dead in the Le Pesant case, as their custom required.
The Jesuits were Catholic priests whose missions lined the St. Lawrence and who, with French officers and officials, mediated conflicts between Indian nations to keep them allied to France.
Pierre Le Moyne d'Iberville was the veteran French sailor and soldier who founded Louisiana with a post at Biloxi Bay.
The Company of the Indies managed France's slave trade and brought nearly 6,000 slaves, mostly men, directly from Africa to Louisiana.
The Natchez were Louisiana Indians who rose against French encroachment, joined by newly arrived slaves, killing or capturing about 500 colonists before the French crushed them.
The Choctaws were rivals of the Natchez who helped the French, along with enslaved blacks promised freedom, crush the Natchez uprising.
The Scots-Irish were descendants of Scots who had settled northern Ireland, about 250,000 of whom came to the colonies and pushed into the backcountry.
About 135,000 Germans, many fleeing war and persecution, settled the colonies, especially Pennsylvania's backcountry, where they kept their own language and customs.

Benjamin Franklin of Philadelphia, entrepreneur, inventor and politician, was the leading American champion of the Enlightenment's useful knowledge and experimentation, inventing an efficient stove and the lightning rod.

column1: What Franklin thought of the backcountry and the Germans
column2: Benjamin Franklin saw the backcountry as draining off surplus eastern people but feared seaboard-backcountry discord and warned that Germans would overrun English Pennsylvania.
Charles Woodmason was an Anglican missionary in the Carolina backcountry who scorned the Scots-Irish as "Ignorant, mean, worthless, beggarly Irish Presbyterians."
Philadelphia was the grandest and most populous colonial seaport, the largest city in the colonies and the second largest in the British Empire.
The Great Wagon Road ran from Philadelphia through western Pennsylvania, Maryland and Virginia into the Carolinas, carrying Scots-Irish and German settlers into the backcountry.
Jemmy was the enslaved man who led nearly 100 Africans in South Carolina's Stono Rebellion, the largest slave revolt of the colonial period.
The philosophes were the leading Enlightenment thinkers, who stressed the power of human reason to reveal the laws of nature and society and promote progress.
Jonathan Edwards was a Calvinist Congregational pastor in Northampton, Massachusetts, whose Great Awakening sermons paired God's grace with terrifying pictures of sinners held over hell.
George Whitefield was the dramatic English "boy preacher" whose two-year tour from Georgia to New Hampshire turned local revivals into the Great Awakening.
The Baptists were the warmest champions of the Great Awakening, drawing its most radical converts and growing in the South and backcountry despite Anglican persecution.
The Presbyterians were a leading northern denomination that split over the Great Awakening yet spread new churches through the South and backcountry.
The Congregationalists, with the Presbyterians the largest northern churchgoing group, split into factions over the Great Awakening.
The Quakers and Anglicans shunned the Great Awakening, and Anglican parsons in the South pushed officials to harass Baptist ministers.
Before 1760 Parliament made no effort to assert its authority over the colonies beyond occasional laws on trade, manufacturing and money, simply assuming its sovereignty covered the empire.
John Dickinson was a young Pennsylvania law student in London, scandalized when the king's ministers spent over 100,000 pounds and got voters "dead drunk" to win an election.
